from uuid import UUID

from application.readings.dto import ReadingDto
from domain.devices.entity import Device
from domain.devices.errors import DeviceNotFoundError
from domain.sensors.ports import SensorPort
from domain.sensors.reading import Reading
from infrastructure.adapters.sensors.selector import select_sensor_adapter
from infrastructure.persistence.device_repository import DeviceRepository
from infrastructure.persistence.reading_repository import ReadingRepository

AdapterFactory = Callable[[Device], SensorPort]


class ReadingService:
    """Use case: resolve device -> pick adapter -> read -> persist -> DTO.

    Depends on the SensorPort abstraction; concrete adapters enter only
    through the selector (the one allowed seam to infrastructure adapters).
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        devices: DeviceRepository,
        readings: ReadingRepository,
        adapter_selector: AdapterFactory = select_sensor_adapter,
    ) -> None:
        self._devices = devices
        self._readings = readings
        self._adapter_selector = adapter_selector

    def take_reading(self, device_id: UUID) -> ReadingDto:
        device = self._require_device(device_id)
        port = self._adapter_selector(device)
        reading = port.read(device)  # adapter errors surface as SensorReadError
        persisted = self._readings.insert(reading)
        return self._to_dto(persisted)

    def list_readings(self, device_id: UUID, limit: int = 20) -> list[ReadingDto]:
        self._require_device(device_id)
        return [self._to_dto(reading) for reading in self._readings.list_for_device(device_id, limit=limit)]

    def _require_device(self, device_id: UUID) -> Device:
        device = self._devices.get_device(device_id)
        if device is None:
            raise DeviceNotFoundError(f"Device {device_id} does not exist")
        return device

    @staticmethod
    def _to_dto(reading: Reading) -> ReadingDto:
        return ReadingDto(
            device_id=reading.device_id,
            value=reading.value,
            unit=reading.unit,
            source=reading.source,
            recorded_at=reading.recorded_at,
        )

{"kind":"tool","id":"Eo2BKceyd8Y","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"docs/patterns/adapter.md","instructions":"Create the Phase 5 Adapter pattern note.","content":"# Adapter — Phase 5

## Problem

Sensor drivers speak foreign dialects. The simulation driver invents plausible values, while the mocked vendor SDK returns a raw payload with nested objects, odd field names (`reading_tenths`, `uom_code`, `captured_epoch_ms`), scaled integers, vendor unit codes (`PCT`, `KLX`), and epoch milliseconds. If business code speaks those dialects directly, every caller re-implements parsing, scaling, and unit conversion, and swapping a vendor means rewriting services. The smell is **business code speaking a foreign protocol**.

## Solution

Adapter converts the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. This phase splits each integration into a **port** (the application-facing interface) and thin **adapters** (the translators):

| Role | In Phase 5 |
|------|------------|
| **Target (port)** | `SensorPort.read(device) -> Reading`, `ActuatorPort.apply(device_id, command, payload)` |
| **Adaptee** | Simulation driver logic, mocked vendor SDK payload |
| **Adapter** | `SimulationSensorAdapter`, `VendorStubSensorAdapter`, `SimulationActuatorAdapter` |
| **Client** | `ReadingService`, the sensors router, the dashboard card |

Every adapter returns the same normalized `Reading` value object (`device_id`, `value`, `unit`, `source`, `recorded_at`). The vendor adapter **translates** only: field names, integer scaling (deci-percent → percent, tent [… 586 characters omitted] n explicit `default_config["protocol"]` wins (`sim` → simulation adapter, `gpio-stub` → vendor-stub adapter); otherwise fall back to `device_family` (`simulation` → simulation adapter, `edge` → vendor-stub adapter). Unknown protocols raise `SensorReadError` (HTTP 400).

`POST /api/sensors/{id}/read` runs: load device (missing → 404) → select adapter → `port.read()` → append to `sensor_readings` → map to `ReadingDto`. Readings are **appended** (`sensor_readings`, indexed on `(device_id, recorded_at DESC)`), so history grows and Phase 6 Strategy can consume real persisted data.

The actuator side ships `ActuatorPort` plus `SimulationActuatorAdapter` now: `apply()` records the command intent in memory and logs it — no GPIO. Phase 9 wraps this exact class with decorators.

## Object adapter, not class adapter

These are **object adapters**: each adapter *has* (or stands in for) the adaptee and implements the port by composition. The GoF class-adapter alternative uses multiple inheritance to adapt an interface; modern code prefers composition because it is looser, works with any adaptee instance, and avoids fragile base classes.

## Code paths

- Ports: `backend/src/domain/sensors/ports.py`, `backend/src/domain/actuators/ports.py`
- Normalized value object: `backend/src/domain/sensors/reading.py`
- Sensor adapters: `backend/src/infrastructure/adapters/sensors/simulation.py`, `vendor_stub.py`
- Selection rule: `backend/src/infrastructure/adapters/sensors/selector.py`
- Actuator stub: `backend/src/infrastructure/adapters/actuators/simulation.py`
- ORM + repository: `backend/src/infrastructure/persistence/models.py` (`ReadingRow`), `reading_repository.py`
- Use case: `backend/src/application/readings/service.py` (+ `dto.py`)
- HTTP endpoints: `backend/src/interfaces/api/sensors.py`
- Sensor card "Read now": `frontend/src/features/sensors/SensorList.tsx`

## Extension exercise (third vendor)

Add a second vendor driver whose raw payload uses yet another shape (for example XML or an epoch in seconds). Write `VendorTwoSensorAdapter(SensorPort)` with its own `translate`, map its protocol key in `select_sensor_adapter`, and keep `Reading`, `sensor_readings`, `ReadingService`, the routes, and the UI untouched — only the new adapter and one selector entry change. That is Adapter's payoff: the boundary absorbs vendor churn.

## What was built

**Domain** (no FastAPI/SQLAlchemy/Pydantic):
- [reading.py](backend/src/domain/sensors/reading.py) — frozen `Reading` (`device_id`, `value`, `unit`, `source`, `recorded_at`, tz-aware enforced)
- [ports.py](backend/src/domain/sensors/ports.py) — `SensorPort.read(device) -> Reading`; [actuators/ports.py](backend/src/domain/actuators/ports.py) — `ActuatorPort.apply(device_id, command, payload)`
- Errors: [SensorReadError](backend/src/domain/sensors/errors.py) (→400), [DeviceNotFoundError](backend/src/domain/devices/errors.py) (→404)

**Adapters** (infrastructure):
- [simulation.py](backend/src/infrastructure/adapters/sensors/simulation.py) — plausible values per device type, `source="simulation"`
- [vendor_stub.py](backend/src/infrastructure/adapters/sensors/vendor_stub.py) — the vendor raw shape is deliberately foreign (nested `sample`, `reading_tenths`, `uom_code` PCT/KLX, `captured_epoch_ms`); pure `translate()` converts scaling (deci-percent→percent, tenths-of-kilolux→lux) and epoch ms→UTC datetime, `source="vendor"` — translation only, no irrigation policy
- [selector.py](backend/src/infrastructure/adapters/sensors/selector.py) — documented rule: explicit `default_config["protocol"]` wins (`sim`/`gpio-stub`), else `device_family` (`simulation`/`edge`)
- [actuators/simulation.py](backend/src/infrastructure/adapters/actuators/simulation.py) — `SimulationActuatorAdapter.apply` records intent in memory + logs; **no GPIO**, ready for Phase 9 decorators

**Persistence & application:** autogenerated migration [64d5e11816a6](backend/alembic/versions/64d5e11816a6_sensor_readings.py) creates `sensor_readings` (FK→`devices`, index `(device_id, recorded_at DESC)`); `ReadingRepository.insert`/`list_for_device` append history; [service.py](backend/src/application/readings/service.py) does load device → select adapter → read → persist → DTO.

**API & UI:** `POST /api/sensors/{id}/read` (201, 404/400) and `GET /api/sensors/{id}/readings?limit=` on the `sensors` tag; [SensorList.tsx](frontend/src/features/sensors/SensorList.tsx) cards have **Read now**, value + color-coded source badge, loading/error states, and load the latest DB reading on mount.

**Q1** (intent + problem):"Adapter makes one interface look like another so classes with incompatible interfaces can work together without either side changing. If business code speaks that dialect directly, every caller ends up parsing payloads, converting units, and translating timestamps; a vendor upgrade or a second vendor then rewrites services instead of adding one class."

**Q2** (participants + translate/not decide):
"Target/port: `SensorPort` (and `ActuatorPort`) — the interface the application expects. Adaptee: the foreign driver, e.g. the mocked vendor SDK payload and the simulation driver. Adapter: `VendorStubSensorAdapter` and `SimulationSensorAdapter`, the translators. Client: `ReadingService` and the sensors router, which only see the port. The adapter translates shape and protocol — field names, scaling (deci-percent → percent, tenths of kilolux → lux), unit codes, timestamps. It must not decide business policy such as 'if moisture < 0.3 then water'; that is domain logic (Strategy in Phase 6)."

**Q3** (object vs class adapter):
"Modern code prefers the object adapter: the adapter holds or stands next to the adaptee and implements the port through composition. Composition is looser — it works with any adaptee instance (or a stub), it can wrap several adaptees, and it avoids fragile inheritance hierarchies. A class adapter uses multiple inheritance to adapt at the type level, which couples the adapter to one adaptee class and is awkward in languages without multiple inheritance. This lab's adapters are object adapters (and the vendor stub even keeps `translate` as a pure function)."

**Q4** (SensorPort + Reading + why depend on port):
"`SensorPort` is the lab's application-facing sensor interface: `read(device) -> Reading`. Adapters return the normalized `Reading` value object (`device_id`, `value`, `unit`, `source`, `recorded_at`, timezone-aware). Application services depend on the port so that drivers can be swapped without touching business code — the vendor SDK or simulation driver can change, be mocked in tests, or be replaced by real hardware later, while `ReadingService`, the routes, and the UI stay unchanged. It also keeps vendor imports out of the application layer."

**Q5** (different raw shapes + source):
"If both adapters already produced the domain shape, there would be nothing to translate and no Adapter to write. The point is that the simulation driver and the vendor stub disagree with the domain and with each other — nested payload with `sample.reading_tenths`, vendor unit codes `PCT`/`KLX`, epoch milliseconds vs plain values — yet both must land in the same `Reading`. That is what proves the translation boundary works. Each adapter stamps `source` (`"simulation"` or `"vendor"`) on the reading it produces, so every row in `sensor_readings` records its provenance and the UI can show a badge distinguishing mocked vendor data from simulated data."

**Q6** (append history + later phase):
"Only the latest value hides trends, and an in-memory value disappears on restart and is invisible to other processes; overwriting a single row destroys history. Appending to `sensor_readings` keeps an audit trail and gives real data to draw charts from and to evaluate policies against (a single point says nothing about whether moisture is falling). Phase 6 (Strategy) consumes this history — policies look at latest/ recent readings per `location_id` zones; Phase 11 (Observer) publishes `reading.created` from this pipeline, and optional Phase 13 charts query the same table."

**Q7** (HTTP statuses + router isolation):
"A missing device is a client error about a resource that does not exist → 404. An adapter failure (malformed vendor payload, unknown unit code) is a bad request against an existing device → 400 with a detail message. The router must never see vendor-shaped types because the whole point of the port is that only adapters know vendor dialects; if the router parsed `reading_tenths` or XML, the translation boundary would leak, and swapping vendors would mean rewriting HTTP handlers."

**Q8** (Adapter vs Facade):
"Adapter changes the shape of an existing interface so two incompatible sides can talk; it typically wraps one adaptee and implements one port. Facade keeps the subsystem as it is but gives callers one simpler entry point — often one method over many classes. Greenhouse example: `VendorStubSensorAdapter` makes the vendor's raw payload look like `SensorPort.read()` (Adapter, this phase). In Phase 7 a facade could expose `GET /api/overview` returning sensors, latest readings, and location configuration through one call (`DashboardFacade.overview()`), even though behind it sit device, reading, and location services (Facade)."

**Q9** (Adapter vs Decorator):
"Both wrap an object, but an adapter presents a different interface than the adaptee — it translates. A decorator implements the same interface as the thing it wraps and only adds behavior while forwarding calls. In this lab `VendorStubSensorAdapter` exposes `SensorPort.read()` while the vendor payload underneath has another shape (Adapter). Phase 9 wraps `SimulationActuatorAdapter` with decorators that still present `ActuatorPort.apply()` but add logging, timing, or retries around it (Decorator)."

**Q10** (policy in adapter trap):
"An adapter should only translate. If it waters 'when moisture < 0.3', the policy is buried in infrastructure: the hard-coded threshold ignores the per-zone thresholds saved with the location configuration, every new policy means editing driver code, the same rule has to be repeated in both adapters, and it cannot be tested or swapped independently. The decision belongs in domain policy chosen per zone/location — Phase 6 Strategy holds interchangeable policies (e.g. threshold-based watering) that read persisted readings and zone thresholds from Phase 4. What stays in the adapter: field mapping, unit conversion, timestamps, and (for actuators) applying a command to the driver."

{"kind":"tool","id":"Nuv6kbyoTkk","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"backend/src/domain/automation/strategy.py","instructions":"Add the AutomationStrategy interface, conservative and aggressive moisture strategies, and the key lookup that rejects unknown keys before any decide call.","content":""""Automation strategies: interchangeable moisture policies behind decide(context).

Strategies are pure. They take a LocationAutomationContext and return a
Recommendation. They never touch the database, actuators, or HTTP types.
Choosing a strategy (get_strategy) is kept separate from running it (decide).
"""

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from dataclasses import dataclass

from domain.automation.context import LocationAutomationContext
from domain.automation.errors import UnknownStrategyError

ACTION_IRRIGATE = "irrigate"
ACTION_WAIT = "wait"
DEFAULT_STRATEGY_KEY = "conservative"


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Recommendation:
    action: str
    reason: str


class AutomationStrategy(ABC):
    key: str

    @abstractmethod
    def decide(self, context: LocationAutomationContext) -> Recommendation:
        """Recommend irrigate or wait for one zone."""
        raise NotImplementedError


class ConservativeMoistureStrategy(AutomationStrategy):
    """Irrigates only when moisture falls below the zone's low threshold."""

    key = "conservative"

    def decide(self, context: LocationAutomationContext) -> Recommendation:
        if context.moisture < context.moisture_low:
            return Recommendation(
                ACTION_IRRIGATE,
                f"Zone {context.zone_name}: moisture {context.moisture:.2f} is below "
                f"the low threshold {context.moisture_low:.2f}",
            )
        return Recommendation(ACTION_WAIT, _wait_reason(context))


class AggressiveMoistureStrategy(AutomationStrategy):
    """Irrigates as soon as moisture falls below the zone's high threshold.

    Differs from the conservative policy inside the band between the low and
    high thresholds: there, conservative waits and aggressive irrigates.
    """

    key = "aggressive"

    def decide(self, context: LocationAutomationContext) -> Recommendation:
        if context.moisture < context.moisture_high:
            return Recommendation(
                ACTION_IRRIGATE,
                f"Zone {context.zone_name}: moisture {context.moisture:.2f} is below "
                f"the high threshold {context.moisture_high:.2f}",
            )
        return Recommendation(ACTION_WAIT, _wait_reason(context))


def _wait_reason(context: LocationAutomationContext) -> str:
    if context.moisture < context.moisture_high:
        return (
            f"Zone {context.zone_name}: moisture {context.moisture:.2f} is within "
            f"{context.moisture_low:.2f}–{context.moisture_high:.2f}"
        )
    return (
        f"Zone {context.zone_name}: moisture {context.moisture:.2f} is above "
        f"the high threshold {context.moisture_high:.2f}"
    )


_STRATEGIES: dict[str, AutomationStrategy] = {
    strategy.key: strategy
    for strategy in (ConservativeMoistureStrategy(), AggressiveMoistureStrategy())
}

STRATEGY_KEYS: tuple[str, ...] = tuple(_STRATEGIES)


def get_strategy(key: str) -> AutomationStrategy:
    """Look up a strategy by key. Unknown keys fail before any decide() call."""
    strategy = _STRATEGIES.get(key)
    if strategy is None:
        raise UnknownStrategyError(f"Unknown automation strategy: {key!r}")
    return strategy

from uuid import UUID

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from domain.automation.rule import AutomationRule
from domain.sensors.reading import Reading

from .models import AutomationRuleRow, DeviceRow, ReadingRow

# Matches MoistureSensorCreator.device_type. Devices are not yet bound to a
# location, so the latest moisture reading is taken across moisture sensors.
MOISTURE_DEVICE_TYPE = "moisture_sensor"


class AutomationRepository:
    def __init__(self, session: Session) -> None:
        self._session = session

    def get_rule(self, location_id: UUID) -> AutomationRule | None:
        row = self._session.scalars(
            select(AutomationRuleRow).where(AutomationRuleRow.location_id == location_id)
        ).first()
        return None if row is None else self._to_domain(row)

    def upsert_rule(self, location_id: UUID, strategy_key: str) -> AutomationRule:
        """Create or update the one rule for a location."""
        now = datetime.now(UTC)
        row = self._session.scalars(
            select(AutomationRuleRow).where(AutomationRuleRow.location_id == location_id)
        ).first()
        if row is None:
            row = AutomationRuleRow(
                location_id=location_id,
                strategy_key=strategy_key,
                parameters={},
                updated_at=now,
            )
            self._session.add(row)
        else:
            row.strategy_key = strategy_key
            row.updated_at = now
        try:
            self._session.commit()
            self._session.refresh(row)
        except Exception:
            self._session.rollback()
            raise
        return self._to_domain(row)

    def latest_moisture_reading(self) -> Reading | None:
        row = self._session.scalars(
            select(ReadingRow)
            .join(DeviceRow, DeviceRow.id == ReadingRow.device_id)
            .where(DeviceRow.device_type == MOISTURE_DEVICE_TYPE)
            .order_by(ReadingRow.recorded_at.desc(), ReadingRow.id.desc())
            .limit(1)
        ).first()
        if row is None:
            return None
        return Reading(
            device_id=row.device_id,
            value=float(row.value),
            unit=row.unit,
            source=row.source,
            recorded_at=row.recorded_at,
        )

    @staticmethod
    def _to_domain(row: AutomationRuleRow) -> AutomationRule:
        return AutomationRule(
            location_id=row.location_id,
            strategy_key=row.strategy_key,
            updated_at=row.updated_at,
        )

        config: LocationConfig,
        strategy: AutomationStrategy,

        reading = self._rules.latest_moisture_reading()
        if reading is None:

) -> RecommendationDto:
    """Evaluate the persisted strategy against the latest moisture and zone thresholds."""

## Problem

Irrigation policy is a choice, not a fixed rule. A conservative grower waits until moisture is clearly low; an aggressive one tops up earlier. If that choice lives as `if strategy == "conservative": ... elif strategy == "aggressive": ...` inside the service or the HTTP router, every new policy edits the same hotspot, and tests must cover every branch combination. The smell is **algorithm and selection logic fused together**.

## Solution

Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface. The client picks one; the context runs it without knowing which one it is.

| Role | In Phase 6 |
|------|------------|
| **Strategy** | `AutomationStrategy.decide(context) -> Recommendation` |
| **Concrete strategies** | `ConservativeMoistureStrategy` (`"conservative"`), `AggressiveMoistureStrategy` (`"aggressive"`) |
| **Context (plain input)** | `LocationAutomationContext`: `location_id`, `zone_name`, `moisture`, `moisture_low`, `moisture_high` (all 0–1 fractions) |
| **Context user / client** | `AutomationService.evaluate()`, which loads the persisted key and builds one context per zone |

Choosing a strategy (`get_strategy(key)`) is separate from running it (`decide`). An unknown key raises `UnknownStrategyError` before any `decide()` call  [… 1,032 characters omitted] ions`), `automation_repository.py`, migration `a1c3e9f07b2d_automation_rules.py`
- API: `backend/src/interfaces/api/automation.py` — `GET` and `PUT /api/locations/{location_id}/automation`, `POST .../automation/evaluate`
- UI: `frontend/src/features/automation/StrategyPanel.tsx` (mounted in `#automation`)
- Tests: `backend/tests/test_automation.py`

## Design decisions

- **Persistence:** a dedicated `automation_rules` table (not columns on `locations`). `location_id` is unique, so each location has exactly one active strategy. Saving an existing location updates its row in place.
- **Thresholds come from `zones`**, never from constants in a strategy class.
- **Evaluation uses the saved key.** The client cannot override it per request. A location with no saved rule uses `conservative` and the response says `is_default`.
- **Units:** sensors report moisture in percent (0–100); thresholds are fractions (0–1). The service converts once, when it builds the context, so strategies only ever see fractions.
- **Multiple zones:** each zone gets its own decision. The location irrigates if any zone asks for water; the reason names that zone.
- **Recommend, don't act:** `decide` returns `irrigate` or `wait`. It never drives a pump. Carrying out the action is Command (Phase 10) on top of actuators.

## Known limitation

Devices are not yet bound to a location (no `location_id` on `devices`), so the "latest moisture" is the newest reading across all moisture sensors. Binding sensors to locations is the natural next step, and the service method that loads the reading is the only place that would change.

## Add-a-third-strategy exercise

Add `FrugalMoistureStrategy` that irrigates only when moisture is below the low threshold **and** the reading is at least 30 minutes old (to avoid watering right after a manual top-up). Steps:

1. Write the class in `domain/automation/strategy.py` with `key = "frugal"` and a `decide` method. Extend `LocationAutomationContext` only if it needs the reading time.
2. Add it to the `_STRATEGIES` tuple. It appears in `available_strategies` and the dropdown with no other changes.
3. Add a unit test next to the others showing it differs from the two existing strategies.

If the router or the service needs an `if key == "frugal"` branch, the design has leaked: move that logic into the strategy.

The questions are all answered in place, but each answer is one compact paragraph of about three to five sentences. They're grounded in the code and cover every part of each question, but they're not long-form. I can expand any of them if you want more depth.

## 1. Why the migration was hand-written, and what "alembic check" proves

**Why by hand:** `alembic revision --autogenerate` works by connecting to a running database, reading its current schema, and diffing it against the SQLAlchemy models. Docker's Postgres wasn't responding, so there was no database to diff against. I wrote the migration `a1c3e9f07b2d` to match the `AutomationRuleRow` model: a `CREATE TABLE automation_rules` with the UUID primary key, a `location_id` foreign key to `locations` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, a unique constraint on `location_id`, a JSONB `parameters` column defaulting to `{}`, and a timestamptz `updated_at` defaulting to `now()`.

**How I checked it:**
- **Offline SQL:** `alembic upgrade --sql` rendered the DDL without a database, and it matched the model.
- **Real apply:** after the database came back, `alembic upgrade head` applied the migration to Postgres (exit 0), and the head became `a1c3e9f07b2d`.
- **Drift check:** `alembic check` compares the migrated database against the model metadata. It reported "No new upgrade operations detected." That means column types, nullability, the foreign key, and the unique constraint all match.

**What it doesn't prove:** I did not run the downgrade (`drop_table`), so the rollback path is untested.

## 2. Moisture comes from the newest reading across all sensors

**The data path:** `sensor_readings` links to `devices`, and `devices` has no `location_id`. The query in `latest_moisture_reading` takes the newest reading among all devices with `device_type = 'moisture_sensor'`, regardless of which location they serve.

**Why it matters:**
- **Cross-location leakage:** if two greenhouses each have a moisture sensor, both locations evaluate against whichever sensor reported last. Each still uses its own zone thresholds, but the moisture input is shared.
- **No staleness check:** a reading from hours ago still drives a decision.

**The fix:** add a `location_id` (or a join table) to devices, have sensor creation and provisioning assign a location, and filter `latest_moisture_reading` by the location being evaluated. The change is contained: the repository query, the service call signature, and a migration. The rest of Phase 6 stays as it is. A reasonable addition would be a maximum reading age, so stale readings are ignored.

**Pattern / focus:** Strategy.

## How to answer

- Use your own wording. Do not paste teaching-example types (for example shipping quotes) as if they were your greenhouse classes.
- When a question asks about *this application*, refer to irrigation (or lighting) policies, location context, and the automation API from the lab.
- Short answers are fine when the question is narrow. Write a few sentences when it asks you to explain or compare.

## A. Pattern

1. State the intent of Strategy in plain language. How does the **context** use a strategy, and why must “choose which algorithm” stay separate from “run the algorithm”?

**Answer:** Strategy lets one algorithm be swapped for another without changing the code that uses it. In this lab the context is `AutomationService`, and it contains no irrigation rule of its own. An evaluation loads the saved `strategy_key` for the location, resolves a strategy object with `get_strategy(key)`, and calls `decide(context)` on it. The service keeps the job of gathering inputs: the location's zones, the latest moisture reading, and the percent-to-fraction conversion.

Choosing and running are kept apart on purpose. `get_strategy` answers “which algorithm?” and only validates: an unregistered key raises `UnknownStrategyError`. `set_strategy` runs that check before it touches the database, so a bad key is never written. `decide` answers “what should happen?” and computes only from the context it receives, with no reads or writes. Because the steps are distinct, each can be tested on its own.

The separation is only real if it survives change. Adding a third strategy means writing one class with a `key` and a `decide` method, then adding it to the registry. `AutomationService` and the router would not change. That is the test this design has to pass.

2. Name the participants (**strategy**, **concrete strategies**, **context**, **client**). What goes wrong when all policies live as `if/elif` inside the context (or inside an HTTP router)?

**Answer:** The participants are the `AutomationStrategy` interface, the concrete `ConservativeMoistureStrategy` and `AggressiveMoistureStrategy`, the context that gathers inputs and delegates (`AutomationService`), and the client that picks a strategy (the saved per-location rule, set through the API).

When policies live as `if/elif` branches, each new policy edits the same lines, so changes collide and a bug in one branch can break others. The branching then spreads into the router, which ends up holding business rules that belong in the domain. Testing gets harder too: checking one policy's behavior means going through the HTTP layer or building the whole service, rather than calling one class with plain numbers. Policy names also leak into the API contract, so renaming or adding a policy becomes a client-visible change.

In this lab the router only parses requests, calls `AutomationService`, and maps `UnknownStrategyError` to 400 and `LocationNotFoundError` to 404. No `if strategy ==` appears in it. The two policies live in separate classes in `domain/automation/strategy.py`.

3. When should you use Strategy, and when should you skip it (one algorithm only; or the variation is a **lifecycle mode** rather than a chosen policy)?

**Answer:** Use Strategy when several interchangeable algorithms answer the same question and the client chooses which applies. Conservative and aggressive irrigation both answer “should this zone be watered?”, and an operator picks one per location. Either policy can replace the other without changing the caller.

Skip Strategy when there is only one algorithm, because the indirection adds code with no benefit. Skip it also when the variation is a lifecycle: the object moves between modes as events happen, for example an actuator going from closed to open to faulted. That is a State problem (Phase 8), because the object changes its own state rather than a client choosing a policy.

A single threshold check is fine as a plain function. Introduce Strategy when the second policy appears, not before.

## B. This phase of the application

4. In this lab, what does a strategy’s `decide(context)` return (action + reason)? Give a concrete difference you implemented (or were required to implement) between **conservative** and **aggressive** on the **same** moisture reading and zone thresholds.

**Answer:** `decide` returns a `Recommendation` with two fields. `action` is `irrigate` or `wait`. `reason` is a human-readable sentence that names the zone and the numbers used. The reason is part of the result on purpose, so an operator can see why the system decided.

The two strategies differ only inside the band between the low and high thresholds. With a zone band of 0.25–0.45 and moisture 0.40, conservative waits with the reason “within 0.25–0.45”, because it irrigates only below the low threshold. Aggressive irrigates with the reason “below the high threshold 0.45”, because it irrigates below the high threshold. Below 0.25 both irrigate, and at or above 0.45 both wait, so the difference shows only in the middle band.

This is why the evaluate endpoint gives different answers for the same reading after a strategy change, which is the behavior the Phase 6 check requires.

5. Where do the numbers in `LocationAutomationContext` (or your equivalent) come from? Why must strategies receive a plain context object, not SQLAlchemy rows or FastAPI types? Why are thresholds read from **zones**, not hardcoded in the strategy class?

**Answer:** `LocationAutomationContext` is built in the application layer. Moisture comes from the newest `sensor_readings` row among moisture sensors, converted from percent (0–100) to a 0–1 fraction. Thresholds come from the location's zones, loaded through the location repository. The context holds the location id, the zone name, the moisture value, and the zone's low and high thresholds, all as plain values.

Strategies receive a frozen dataclass rather than ORM rows or FastAPI request objects for three reasons. The first is dependency direction: the domain must not import SQLAlchemy or FastAPI, or the policies can't be used or tested without a web stack. The second is testability: a unit test can build a context from three numbers and assert on the result. The third is safety: an ORM object can lazy-load relationships or change mid-decision, while a frozen value cannot.

Thresholds come from zones because the operator sets them per zone in Phase 4. A hardcoded constant would ignore those settings and force every zone into one band. There is one known gap: moisture is the newest reading across all moisture sensors, because devices aren't yet tied to a location. That is a limitation of the current data model, not a design choice.

6. The active `strategy_key` is **persisted** per `location_id` (for example in `automation_rules`). Why must `POST .../automation/evaluate` use the **saved** key rather than a key the client sends only in that request? What happens on the next evaluate after the operator changes strategy but moisture stays the same?

**Answer:** The key is part of the location's configuration, stored in `automation_rules` with one row per location. If the evaluate request could carry its own key, the answer would depend on which client asked, and the saved configuration would stop describing what the system does. The saved key is the single source of truth.

Suppose the operator switches from conservative to aggressive and moisture stays at 0.40 against a band of 0.25–0.45. The next evaluate returns irrigate where it returned wait before, because the aggressive policy acts at any reading below the high threshold. The sensor didn't change; the policy did. The response echoes the `strategy_key` that was used, so every recommendation traces back to the policy that produced it.

Switching is a single update of one row. The unique constraint on `location_id` guarantees one row per location, so there is never more than one active strategy at a time.

7. Strategy **recommends** (irrigate / wait). It should not itself start a pump. Why keep **decide** separate from **execute**? Which later pattern is meant to carry out the action?

**Answer:** `decide` is pure. It reads a context and returns a recommendation, so it can be unit-tested with numbers, logged, and reviewed without any hardware present. Executing an action changes the world: it opens a valve, spends water, and wears equipment. Keeping the two apart means a recommendation can be checked, overridden by an operator, rate-limited, or logged before anything moves.

Mixing them creates the failure the separation prevents. A strategy that waters directly cannot be tested without an actuator, and a bad threshold would cause real water use with no chance to intervene.

The pattern meant to carry out the action is Command (Phase 10). A command object wraps an actuator request, such as “open the valve for two minutes”, and can be queued, logged, and undone. It sits above the Phase 5 actuator adapter and below the recommendation, so the path is recommendation → command → actuator.

## C. Compare, contrast, and scenarios

8. Contrast Strategy with **State** (Phase 8). Both delegate to an object with the same shape. Who typically **changes** the active object, and is the variation a **policy** or a **lifecycle**?

**Answer:** Both patterns delegate calls to a contained object that shares a method shape, which is why they look alike. The difference is who changes the active object, and why.

In Strategy, the client chooses the object, usually once, based on configuration. An operator selects a policy for a location. The choices are peers: they don't know about each other and don't transition into one another. The variation is a policy, answering “how should we decide?”

In State, the object itself moves between states as events occur, and each state knows which transitions are legal. An actuator goes from closed to open to faulted, and an open actuator cannot be opened again. The variation is a lifecycle, answering “what can happen now, given where we are?”

9. Contrast Strategy with **Adapter** (Phase 5) and with **Builder** (Phase 4). Which one translates a foreign API, which one assembles a valid aggregate, and which one swaps an algorithm?

**Answer:** Adapter translates a foreign interface into the one the application expects. In this lab a vendor raw payload with nested fields and scaled integers becomes a normalized `Reading`. Its job is shape conversion, so business code never sees the vendor's format.

Builder assembles a valid aggregate step by step. `LocationConfigBuilder` collects a name and zones, and `build()` validates them: names are required and unique, thresholds fall between 0 and 1, and low must be below high. The builder guarantees that only a valid configuration exists. It translates nothing and chooses between no alternatives.

Strategy swaps an algorithm. The conservative and aggressive `decide` methods implement the same contract with different rules, and the caller picks one. In short: Adapter translates, Builder assembles, Strategy swaps.

10. A classmate writes one “mega-strategy” that still contains `if conservative` / `if aggressive` inside a single class. Another strategy class calls the actuator adapter to water immediately. Explain why each is a trap.

**Answer:** The mega-strategy repeats the mistake Strategy exists to fix, just moved into one class. Each new policy adds another branch, every change touches the same method, and tests must cover every combination of branches. Splitting into one class per policy behind `decide` makes each rule testable on its own and lets a new policy arrive without editing existing ones.

A strategy that calls the actuator adapter to water immediately collapses the separation between recommending and acting. It cannot be tested without hardware, skips the review or rate limit an operator would expect, and turns a bad threshold directly into water use. The correct design is for strategies to return a recommendation, with the action going through a Command object that can be logged, queued, and blocked.

Both traps share a root cause: business decisions are mixed with other concerns. In one case the concerns are other policies, and in the other they are physical side effects. Keeping each concern in its own object is what makes the system safe to change.

> 1. Why the migration was hand-written, and what "alembic check" proves
> Why by hand: alembic revision --autogenerate works by connecting to a running database, reading its current schema, and diffing it against the SQLAlchemy models. Docker's Postgres wasn't responding, so there was no database to diff against. I wrote the migration a1c3e9f07b2d to match the AutomationRuleRow model: a CREATE TABLE automation_rules with the UUID primary key, a location_id foreign key to locations with ON DELETE CASCADE, a unique constraint on location_id, a JSONB parameters column defaulting to {}, and a timestamptz updated_at defaulting to now().
> 
> How I checked it:
> 
> Offline SQL: alembic upgrade --sql rendered the DDL without a database, and it matched the model.
> Real apply: after the database came back, alembic upgrade head applied the migration to Postgres (exit 0), and the head became a1c3e9f07b2d.
> Drift check: alembic check compares the migrated database against the model metadata. It reported "No new upgrade operations detected." That means column types, nullability, the foreign key, and the unique constraint all match.
> What it doesn't prove: I did not run the downgrade (drop_table), so the rollback path is untested.
> 
> 2. Moisture comes from the newest reading across all sensors
> The data path: sensor_readings links to devices, and devices has no location_id. The query in latest_moisture_reading takes the newest reading among all devices with device_type = 'moisture_sensor', regardless of which location they serve.
> 
> Why it matters:
> 
> Cross-location leakage: if two greenhouses each have a moisture sensor, both locations evaluate against whichever sensor reported last. Each still uses its own zone thresholds, but the moisture input is shared.
> No staleness check: a reading from hours ago still drives a decision.
> The fix: add a location_id (or a join table) to devices, have sensor creation and provisioning assign a location, and filter latest_moisture_reading by the location being evaluated. The change is contained: the repository query, the service call signature, and a migration. The rest of Phase 6 stays as it is. A reasonable addition would be a maximum reading age, so stale readings are ignored.

**Why the migration was hand-written**

Autogenerate needs a live database. It connects, reads the current schema, and diffs it against the SQLAlchemy models. Docker Desktop's Linux engine went down during the Freebuff restart. Port 5433 still accepted connections, but the Postgres handshake timed out. Later the engine's named pipe disappeared, and the machine ran low on memory. With no database to diff against, I wrote the migration from the model by hand.

Once Docker came back, I could check the hand-written file. `alembic check` loads the migrated schema from the database and compares it to the model metadata. It reported no differences, so the table, columns, foreign key, and unique constraint match. It doesn't test the downgrade, which I haven't run.

**Why moisture is taken across all sensors**

The cause is in the data model. In Phase 2 sensors were stored in `devices` with no location. In Phase 4 locations and zones were added as a separate aggregate, and nothing linked devices to locations. Phase 5 then wrote readings to `sensor_readings` keyed by device. So the database has no path from a reading to a location.

Phase 6 needed a moisture value for each location. With no link available, I used the simplest query: the newest reading among all moisture sensors. That is why two greenhouses share one moisture input. The missing staleness check has a separate cause: the query orders by `recorded_at` but never filters on age.

The real fix is the missing link. Adding `location_id` to `devices`, assigning it when sensors are created, and filtering the moisture query by location would address both problems.

Progress note:
The questions are all answered in place, but each answer is one compact paragraph of about three to five sentences. They're grounded in the code and cover every part of each question, but they're not long-form. I can expand any of them if you want more depth.

## 1. Why the migration was hand-written, and what "alembic check" proves

**Why by hand:** `alembic revision --autogenerate` works by connecting to a running database, reading its current schema, and diffing it against the SQLAlchemy models. Docker's Postgres wasn't responding, so there was no database to diff against. I wrote the migration `a1c3e9f07b2d` to match the `AutomationRuleRow` model: a `CREATE TABLE automation_rules` with the UUID primary key, a `location_id` foreign key to `locations` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, a unique constraint on `location_id`, a JSONB `parameters` column defaulting to `{}`, and a timestamptz `updated_at` defaulting to `now()`.

**How I checked it:**
- **Offline SQL:** `alembic upgrade --sql` rendered the DDL without a database, and it matched the model.
- **Real apply:** after the database came back, `alembic upgrade head` applied the migration to Postgres (exit 0), and the head became `a1c3e9f07b2d`.
- **Drift check:** `alembic check` compares the migrated database against the model metadata. It reported "No new upgrade operations detected." That means column types, nullability, the foreign key, and the unique constraint all match.

**What it doesn't prove:** I did not run the downgrade (`drop_table`), so the rollback path is untested.

## 2. Moisture comes from the newest reading across all sensors

**The data path:** `sensor_readings` links to `devices`, and `devices` has no `location_id`. The query in `latest_moisture_reading` takes the newest reading among all devices with `device_type = 'moisture_sensor'`, regardless of which location they serve.

**Why it matters:**
- **Cross-location leakage:** if two greenhouses each have a moisture sensor, both locations evaluate against whichever sensor reported last. Each still uses its own zone thresholds, but the moisture input is shared.
- **No staleness check:** a reading from hours ago still drives a decision.

**The fix:** add a `location_id` (or a join table) to devices, have sensor creation and provisioning assign a location, and filter `latest_moisture_reading` by the location being evaluated. The change is contained: the repository query, the service call signature, and a migration. The rest of Phase 6 stays as it is. A reasonable addition would be a maximum reading age, so stale readings are ignored.

from application.automation.service import AutomationService
from application.overview.dto import (
    DeviceCountsDto,
    LocationOverviewDto,
    LocationSummaryDto,
    OverviewRecommendationDto,
    ReadingSummaryDto,
)
from domain.locations.errors import LocationNotFoundError
from infrastructure.persistence.device_repository import DeviceRepository
from infrastructure.persistence.location_repository import LocationRepository
from infrastructure.persistence.reading_repository import ReadingRepository


class LocationOverviewFacade:
    """A single read entry point; strategy policy remains in AutomationService."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        locations: LocationRepository,
        devices: DeviceRepository,
        readings: ReadingRepository,
        automation: AutomationService,
    ) -> None:
        self._locations = locations
        self._devices = devices
        self._readings = readings
        self._automation = automation

    def get_overview(self, location_id: UUID) -> LocationOverviewDto:
        config = self._locations.get_config(location_id)
        if config is None:
            raise LocationNotFoundError(f"Location {location_id} does not exist")

        counts = self._devices.count_by_role()
        readings = self._readings.latest_per_sensor()
        recommendation = self._automation.evaluate(location_id)
        return LocationOverviewDto(
            location=LocationSummaryDto(id=location_id, name=config.location.name),
            device_counts=DeviceCountsDto(sensor=counts.get("sensor", 0), actuator=counts.get("actuator", 0)),
            latest_readings=[
                ReadingSummaryDto(
                    device_id=reading.device_id,
                    value=reading.value,
                    unit=reading.unit,
                    recorded_at=reading.recorded_at,
                )
                for reading in readings
            ],
            strategy_key=recommendation.strategy_key,
            last_recommendation=OverviewRecommendationDto(
                action=recommendation.action, reason=recommendation.reason

{"kind":"tool","id":"fxRycuLIskw","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"docs/patterns/facade.md","instructions":"Document the Phase 7 facade design, database queries, and limitations.","content":"# Facade — location overview

`LocationOverviewFacade.get_overview(location_id)` gives the HTTP handler one entry point for a dashboard read model. It coordinates the location, device and reading repositories and delegates the recommendation to `AutomationService`; it does not implement sensor translation, strategy policy or persistence. The handler knows only the facade, and the UI uses one overview request rather than assembling multiple responses.

The facade reads the existing `locations`, `zones`, `devices`, `sensor_readings`, and `automation_rules` tables. No new business table, view, or migration is needed. `last_recommendation` is computed on each GET, not a stored history item; the active strategy is the saved key or the existing default. Refreshing the overview fetches current database values.

Device counts are grouped in one query. Latest readings use a window function to select one row per sensor in one query, rather than making a query for every device (the N+1 problem). The automation service performs its own bounded set of queries. Results from concurrent writes can change between these queries; the response is not a transactionally consistent snapshot.

**Important scope limitation:** devices currently have no location or zone association. Counts and readings are therefore global, not location-specific, and the automation service also evaluates the newest global moisture reading. The API schema and dashboard state this explicitly; do not use the result as location-isolated automation. The route does scope the location, zones and strategy by `location_id`. Fixing device ownership requires a separate schema and workflow change, outside the no-new-business-schema scope of this phase. No freshness limit is currently applied to moisture readings.

import os

from application.overview.dependencies import get_overview_facade

from infrastructure.persistence.models import DeviceRow, LocationRow, ReadingRow

def test_handler_uses_facade_and_documents_schema():
    location_id = uuid4()

    class FakeFacade:
        def get_overview(self, requested_id: UUID) -> LocationOverviewDto:
            assert requested_id == location_id
            return LocationOverviewDto(

                device_counts=DeviceCountsDto(sensor=0, actuator=0),
                latest_readings=[],
                strategy_key="conservative",
                last_recommendation=OverviewRecommendationDto(action="wait", reason="No reading"),

    app.dependency_overrides[get_overview_facade] = lambda: FakeFacade()

            schema = client.get("/openapi.json").json()
            operation = schema["paths"]["/api/locations/{location_id}/overview"]["get"]
            assert operation["responses"]["200"]["content"]["application/json"]["schema"]["$ref"].endswith(
                "/LocationOverviewDto"
            )
            assert "404" in operation["responses"]
            assert client.get("/scalar").status_code == 200
    finally:
        app.dependency_overrides.pop(get_overview_facade, None)


def test_missing_location_is_404_and_other_errors_are_not_hidden():
    class FakeFacade:
        def get_overview(self, location_id: UUID) -> LocationOverviewDto:
            raise LocationNotFoundError(f"Location {location_id} does not exist")

    app.dependency_overrides[get_overview_facade] = lambda: FakeFacade()

            assert client.get(f"/api/locations/{uuid4()}/overview").status_code == 404
    finally:

    class BrokenFacade:

    app.dependency_overrides[get_overview_facade] = lambda: BrokenFacade()
    try:
        with TestClient(app, raise_server_exceptions=False) as client:
            assert client.get(f"/api/locations/{uuid4()}/overview").status_code == 500
    finally:
        app.dependency_overrides.pop(get_overview_facade, None)


@pytest.mark.skipif(os.getenv("RUN_DB_INTEGRATION") != "1", reason="requires PostgreSQL")
def test_overview_returns_strategy_and_readings():
    location_id: UUID | None = None
    device_ids: list[UUID] = []
    queries: list[str] = []

    def count_query(conn, cursor, statement, parameters, context, executemany):
        if statement.lstrip().upper().startswith("SELECT"):
            queries.append(statement)

    try:
        with TestClient(app) as client:
            created = client.post("/api/locations/config", json={
                "location_name": f"Overview test {uuid4()}",
                "zones": [{"name": "Bench", "moisture_threshold_low": 0.25,
                           "moisture_threshold_high": 0.45, "schedule": {}}],
            })
            assert created.status_code == 201
            location_id = UUID(created.json()["location"]["id"])
            assert client.get(f"/api/locations/{uuid4()}/overview").status_code == 404

            with SessionLocal() as session:
                for index in range(3):
                    device = DeviceRow(device_type="moisture_sensor", role="sensor", device_family="simulation")
                    session.add(device)
                    session.flush()
                    device_ids.append(device.id)
                    for value, minutes in [(10.0, 0), (40.0, 1)]:
                        session.add(ReadingRow(
                            device_id=device.id, value=value + index, unit="percent", source="simulation",
                            recorded_at=datetime(9990, 1, 1, tzinfo=UTC) + timedelta(minutes=minutes),
                        ))
                session.commit()

            assert client.put(f"/api/locations/{location_id}/automation", json={"strategy_key": "conservative"}).status_code == 200
            event.listen(engine, "before_cursor_execute", count_query)
            try:
                first = client.get(f"/api/locations/{location_id}/overview")
            finally:
                event.remove(engine, "before_cursor_execute", count_query)
            assert first.status_code == 200
            overview = first.json()
            assert overview["location"] == {"id": str(location_id), "name": created.json()["location"]["name"]}
            assert overview["device_counts"]["sensor"] >= 3
            readings = {r["device_id"]: r for r in overview["latest_readings"]}
            for index, device_id in enumerate(device_ids):
                assert readings[str(device_id)]["value"] == 40.0 + index
                assert readings[str(device_id)]["unit"] == "percent"
                assert "recorded_at" in readings[str(device_id)]
            assert overview["strategy_key"] == "conservative"
            assert overview["last_recommendation"]["action"] == "wait"

","newString":"1. State the intent of Facade in plain language. What problem appears when every HTTP handler (or every UI screen) repeats the same multi-step dance across repositories and services?

**Answer:** Facade gives a caller one higher-level operation for a task that requires several collaborators. Instead of knowing how to gather locations, devices, readings, and automation information, a caller asks for a location overview and receives a result shaped for that use case.

When every handler or screen repeats that orchestration, each copy can call steps in a different order or apply different error handling. A change to the subsystem then requires updating every copy, and one forgotten caller may produce inconsistent results. Centralizing the coordination makes the sequence easier to test and change without forcing all callers to know the details.

**Answer:** A facade should not become a god object that owns every rule and implements every operation in the application. Its responsibility is to coordinate the collaborators needed for one use case and assemble their results, not replace those collaborators.

In this app the overview facade calls the automation service, which delegates irrigation decisions to the selected Strategy. Sensor adapters translate raw sensor data into normalized readings; repositories and the database handle persistence and queries. Keeping those responsibilities separate means the overview can change without copying or rewriting the policy, adapter, or database implementation.
","allowMultiple":false},{"oldString":"3. When should you use Facade, and when should you skip it (a single repository call is enough; or you actually need to **translate** a mismatched interface)?
","newString":"3. When should you use Facade, and when should you skip it (a single repository call is enough; or you actually need to **translate** a mismatched interface)?

**Answer:** Use a facade when a use case regularly requires coordinating several subsystem operations and clients benefit from a stable, simpler entry point. The location overview is a good example: it combines location information, device and reading summaries, and a strategy recommendation.

Skip the extra layer when a caller only needs a simple repository operation and there is no meaningful coordination to hide. If the problem is that a vendor component exposes an incompatible data shape or protocol, use an Adapter to translate it; a Facade is not a substitute for that translation. The two can work together, because a facade can coordinate a subsystem that itself uses adapters.
","allowMultiple":false},{"oldString":"4. What does `GET /api/locations/{location_id}/overview` return? Name the main pieces of the overview DTO (location, device counts, latest readings, strategy key, last recommendation). Why is overview scoped by `location_id`?
","newString":"4. What does `GET /api/locations/{location_id}/overview` return? Name the main pieces of the overview DTO (location, device counts, latest readings, strategy key, last recommendation). Why is overview scoped by `location_id`?

**Answer:** It returns a location object with its ID and name, counts of sensors and actuators, the latest reading per sensor with its device ID, value, unit and timestamp, the active strategy key, and a recommendation with action and reason. The recommendation is computed on each request by the existing automation service; despite the field name `last_recommendation`, it is not a saved historical result. A missing location returns 404.

The path uses `location_id` because location configuration, zones, and the saved strategy belong to a particular location. There is an important current limitation: devices have no location association, so the displayed device counts and latest readings are global, and the automation service uses the latest global moisture reading. The dashboard and API schema label this rather than pretending those fields are location-specific. A future association is needed for true location isolation.
","allowMultiple":false},{"oldString":"5. Why does this phase **not** require a new business table? What already exists from Phases 2–6 that the facade only **composes**?

**Answer:** The overview is a read model, not a new business entity that needs its own durable record. The existing database already contains devices from the factory phases, locations and zones from Builder, sensor reading history from Adapter, and per-location automation rules from Strategy.

The facade obtains those existing facts through repositories and asks the automation service for a recommendation. It combines the answers into a DTO for the dashboard without copying the data to a new business table. No view or schema migration was needed; the current recommendation is calculated on demand instead of stored.
","allowMultiple":false},{"oldString":"6. The overview HTTP handler should call **only** the facade, not reading/strategy/device repositories directly. Why? How does that help tests and later changes to the query shape?
","newString":"6. The overview HTTP handler should call **only** the facade, not reading/strategy/device repositories directly. Why? How does that help tests and later changes to the query shape?

**Answer:** The handler is an HTTP boundary: it accepts a location ID, delegates to one facade, and translates a missing-location error into 404. It does not need to know which repositories to call, how many queries are used, or how the automation service evaluates a recommendation.

A handler test can replace one facade with a fake and check the response and error mapping. The facade and repository can then be tested separately. If the reading query later changes to a join or devices become associated with locations, that work can remain behind the same facade and response contract rather than being repeated in every handler.
","allowMultiple":false},{"oldString":"7. The Overview page should make **one** fetch and render cards from the DTO. Why must the React page not stitch five API calls together to build the same snapshot? How does a new reading or a saved strategy show up on overview without extra frontend glue?
","newString":"7. The Overview page should make **one** fetch and render cards from the DTO. Why must the React page not stitch five API calls together to build the same snapshot? How does a new reading or a saved strategy show up on overview without extra frontend glue?

**Answer:** One overview request keeps subsystem choreography on the server. If React made separate calls for the location, devices, readings, rule and recommendation, each screen would have to coordinate loading, failures, and result mapping itself. Separate requests could also observe different moments in time, although a single overview request alone does not guarantee a transactionally consistent database snapshot either.

On each overview GET, the facade queries the current data and asks the automation service to evaluate the saved strategy. The page displays the returned DTO without calculating the policy itself. A new reading or saved strategy appears on the next load or when the operator presses **Load / refresh**; the page does not currently refresh automatically when another panel changes data.
","allowMultiple":false},{"oldString":"8. Contrast Facade with **Adapter**. One makes an existing interface usable; the other makes a subsystem simpler to call. Which is which, and how do both appear in this greenhouse app (Phase 5 vs Phase 7)?

**Answer:** Adapter translates an existing incompatible interface into a contract the application can use. In Phase 5, simulation and vendor sensor adapters turn differently shaped raw data into normalized readings expected by the sensor port, so application services need not understand vendor fields.

Facade instead offers a simpler entry point to a group of collaborators. In Phase 7, the overview facade coordinates repositories and the automation service and returns one DTO to the handler. It does not translate a vendor protocol itself; it can use data that has already passed through an adapter.
","allowMultiple":false},{"oldString":"9. This phase mentions **N+1** queries. What is an N+1 problem in an overview that lists latest readings for many devices, and what can the facade (or its repository) do about it without putting SQL in the router?
","newString":"9. This phase mentions **N+1** queries. What is an N+1 problem in an overview that lists latest readings for many devices, and what can the facade (or its repository) do about it without putting SQL in the router?

**Answer:** An N+1 problem would occur if the server first queried N sensors and then ran one additional latest-reading query for each sensor. As the sensor count grows, the number of database round trips grows with it, slowing the overview even though the client made only one HTTP request.

Here the reading repository uses a SQL window function, partitioned by device and ordered by timestamp and ID, to select the latest reading for each sensor in one query. The device repository obtains role counts with a grouped query. The facade coordinates those operations while SQL stays in the repository, not the router; an integration test checks that the total number of SELECTs remains bounded for several sensors.
","allowMultiple":false},{"oldString":"10. A classmate hides every error behind a generic “overview failed,” so a missing location, a DB outage, and a strategy error look the same. Why is that a trap for a facade?
","newString":"10. A classmate hides every error behind a generic “overview failed,” so a missing location, a DB outage, and a strategy error look the same. Why is that a trap for a facade?

**Answer:** These errors mean different things and need different responses. A missing location is a client-visible 404, while a database outage is a server-side failure that may require operational attention; an invalid stored strategy indicates an application or configuration problem. Calling all of them “overview failed” makes diagnosis and appropriate client behavior harder and may mislead the operator.

The facade should preserve meaningful failures rather than silently returning an empty overview. This handler catches the specific missing-location error and maps it to 404; other unexpected errors propagate as server errors rather than being misreported as a missing location. Production logging and safe, more specific error responses could improve diagnostics without exposing sensitive internal details.

+# Facade — location overview
+
+`LocationOverviewFacade.get_overview(location_id)` gives the HTTP handler one entry point for a dashboard read model. It coordinates the location, device and reading repositories and delegates the recommendation to `AutomationService`; it does not implement sensor translation, strategy policy or persistence. The handler knows only the facade, and the UI uses one overview request rather than assembling multiple responses.
+
+The facade reads the existing `locations`, `zones`, `devices`, `sensor_readings`, and `automation_rules` tables. No new business table, view, or migration is needed. `last_recommendation` is computed on each GET, not a stored history item; the active strategy is the saved key or the existing default. Refreshing the overview fetches current database values.
+
+Device counts are grouped in one query. Latest readings use a window function to select one row per sensor in one query, rather than making a query for every device (the N+1 problem). The automation service performs its own bounded set of queries. Results from concurrent writes can change between these queries; the response is not a transactionally consistent snapshot.
+
+**Important scope limitation:** devices currently have no location or zone association. Counts and readings are therefore global, not location-specific, and the automation service also evaluates the newest global moisture reading. The API schema and dashboard state this explicitly; do not use the result as location-isolated automation. The route does scope the location, zones and strategy by `location_id`. Fixing device ownership requires a separate schema and workflow change, outside the no-new-business-schema scope of this phase. No freshness limit is currently applied to moisture readings.

+import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
+import { ACTIVE_LOCATION_STORAGE_KEY, fetchOverview, type LocationOverviewDto } from "../../services/api";
+
+export function OverviewPanel() {
+  const [draftId, setDraftId] = useState(() => window.localStorage.getItem(ACTIVE_LOCATION_STORAGE_KEY) ?? "");
+  const [locationId, setLocationId] = useState(draftId.trim());
+  const [refresh, setRefresh] = useState(0);
+  const [overview, setOverview] = useState<LocationOverviewDto | null>(null);
+  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
+  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
+
+  useEffect(() => {
+    if (!locationId) {
+      setOverview(null);
+      setError(null);
+      setLoading(false);
+      return;
+    }
+    let cancelled = false;
+    setOverview(null);
+    setError(null);
+    setLoading(true);
+    // Defer the request so React StrictMode's development-only setup/cleanup does not fetch twice.
+    const timer = window.setTimeout(() => {
+      fetchOverview(locationId)
+        .then((result) => { if (!cancelled) setOverview(result); })
+        .catch((err: unknown) => {
+          if (!cancelled) setError(err instanceof Error ? err.message : "Unable to load overview.");
+        })
+        .finally(() => { if (!cancelled) setLoading(false); });
+    }, 0);
+    return () => { cancelled = true; window.clearTimeout(timer); };
+  }, [locationId, refresh]);
+
+  function handleLoad(event: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
+    event.preventDefault();
+    const nextId = draftId.trim();
+    if (nextId === locationId) setRefresh((value) => value + 1);
+    else setLocationId(nextId);
+  }
+
+  return (
+    <div className="mt-4 space-y-4">
+      <form className="flex flex-wrap items-end gap-2" onSubmit={handleLoad}>
+        <div className="min-w-0 flex-1">
+          <label htmlFor="overview-location-id" className="mb-1 block text-sm font-medium text-slate-700">Location ID</label>
+          <input id="overview-location-id" value={draftId} onChange={(event) => setDraftId(event.target.value)}
+            placeholder="Paste a location ID" className="w-full rounded-md border border-slate-300 px-3 py-2 font-mono text-xs" />
+        </div>
+        <button type="submit" className="rounded-md border border-emerald-600 px-3 py-2 text-sm text-emerald-700">Load / refresh</button>
+      </form>
+      {!locationId && <p className="text-sm text-slate-500">Save a location configuration or enter its ID to see its overview.</p>}
+      {loading && <p className="text-sm text-slate-500" role="status">Loading overview…</p>}
+      {error && <p className="rounded-md bg-red-50 p-3 text-sm text-red-700" role="alert">{error}</p>}
+      {overview && (
+        <div className="space-y-3" aria-live="polite">
+          <h3 className="font-semibold text-slate-900">{overview.location.name}</h3>
+          <p className="text-xs text-amber-800">Device counts and readings are global: devices are not yet assigned to locations. Recommendations use the latest global moisture reading.</p>
+          <section className="rounded-md bg-slate-50 p-3 text-sm">
+            <h4 className="font-semibold">Devices (global)</h4>
+            <p>Sensors: {overview.device_counts.sensor} · Actuators: {overview.device_counts.actuator}</p>
+          </section>
+          <section className="rounded-md bg-slate-50 p-3 text-sm">
+            <h4 className="font-semibold">Latest sensor readings (global)</h4>
+            {overview.latest_readings.length === 0 ? <p>No readings recorded yet.</p> : (
+              <ul className="space-y-2">
+                {overview.latest_readings.map((reading) => (
+                  <li key={reading.device_id}>
+                    <span>{reading.value} {reading.unit}</span>
+                    <p className="break-all text-xs text-slate-500">{reading.device_id} · {new Date(reading.recorded_at).toLocaleString()}</p>
+                  </li>
+                ))}
+              </ul>
+            )}
+          </section>
+          <section className="rounded-md bg-slate-50 p-3 text-sm">
+            <h4 className="font-semibold">Active strategy</h4>
+            <p>{overview.strategy_key ?? "None"}</p>
+          </section>
+          <section className="rounded-md bg-slate-50 p-3 text-sm">
+            <h4 className="font-semibold">Current recommendation</h4>
+            {overview.last_recommendation ? <p>{overview.last_recommendation.action}: {overview.last_recommendation.reason}</p> : <p>No recommendation available.</p>}
+          </section>
+        </div>
+      )}
+    </div>
+  );
+}
